BG:B001323.description: Nicholas Joseph Begich Sr. was an American politician, school counselor, and school administrator. He served in the Alaska state senate for eight years before being elected in 1970 as a member of the United States House of Representatives from Alaska. He is presumed to have died in the crash of a light aircraft in Alaska in October 1972; his body was never found. He was a member of the Democratic Party.

BG:A000055.description: Robert Brown Aderholt is an American politician and attorney from Alabama. A socially conservative member of the Republican Party and a member of the Tea Party Caucus, he is currently serving as a U.S. representative, representing Alabama's 4th congressional district since 1997. The district includes most of Tuscaloosa County north of the Black Warrior River, as well as Birmingham's far northern suburbs in Walker County and the southern suburbs of Huntsville and Decatur.

BG:W000809.description: Stephen Allen Womack is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Arkansas's 3rd congressional district since 2011. The district covers much of northwestern Arkansas, including Fort Smith, Fayetteville, Springdale, and Womack's hometown of Rogers. Before he was elected to Congress, Womack was mayor of Rogers. He is a member of the Republican Party.

BG:H001090.tier_writeup: Josh Harder is a Democratic incumbent from California’s 9th district who serves on the Appropriations Committee and is a vice‑chair of the New Democrat Coalition. In the 119th Congress he voted against the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act (2024‑04‑20) and supported the Israel Security Assistance Support Act (2024‑05‑16), showing a willingness to fund Israel. His only clear anti‑Israel vote was an amendment on 2026‑07‑15 that sought to prohibit funds for Israel, but that single vote is outweighed by multiple pro‑aid votes and by the fact that his anti‑votes often aligned with his party’s majority position. While he has four defections on Iran‑related funding, those do not translate into a consistent anti‑intervention stance on Israel. He receives no known AIPAC money, but his voting pattern and lack of leadership‑defying discharge petitions on the Israel issue suggest he is not a reliable anti‑establishment ally on this core focus.
BG:H001090.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on Israel aid is mixed, including votes that supported large military assistance and only one isolated anti‑aid vote.

BG:K000389.tier_writeup: Ro Khanna is a sitting member of Congress from California who has established a strong record of opposing U.S. military intervention, particularly regarding Israel. In the 119th Congress, he voted against the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, a direct break from the Democratic party line that provided $14.3 billion in military aid. He has also sponsored and cosponsored numerous War Powers Resolution measures directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities in Iran, Lebanon, and the Houthis. Khanna signed four discharge petitions, including H.Res. 164 and H.Res. 250, which are significant acts of defiance against his own party's Speaker and Rules Committee. His voting record shows 8 party defections to the anti-intervention side, with an anti-ratio of 0.67 on focus votes. He has no tracked contributions from the Israel lobby and was not endorsed by TrackAIPAC. His recent public statements, including a declaration for 'Zero Aid to Israel' at a DNC meeting, align with his legislative record. He is a reliable ally who has demonstrated the willingness to incur political costs to oppose foreign wars and arms transfers.
BG:K000389.tier_bottom_line: Counts as anti-establishment because he has consistently voted against his own party to block military aid to Israel and signed multiple discharge petitions to bypass Democratic leadership on war powers.

BG:O000019.description: Jay Phillip Obernolte is an American politician and businessman serving as the U.S. representative for California's 23rd district since 2021, when it was numbered as the 8th district. A Republican, he was previously a member of the California State Assembly representing the 33rd district. Before serving in the Assembly, Obernolte served on the city council and was the mayor of Big Bear Lake, California. He is the owner, president, and technical director of FarSight Studios, an American video game developer.

BG:S000344.description: Bradley James Sherman is an American accountant and politician serving as the U.S. representative for California's 32nd congressional district. A member of the Democratic Party, he first entered Congress in 1997. Sherman represented California's 24th congressional district for three terms, California's 27th congressional district for five terms, and California's 30th congressional district for five terms. BG:S001156.description: Linda Teresa Sánchez is an American politician and former labor lawyer serving as the U.S. representative for California's 38th congressional district since 2013. A member of the Democratic Party, she was first elected to Congress in 2002 in California's 39th congressional district. Sánchez serves on the Ways and Means Committee; she was the ranking member on the House Ethics Committee until 2017. In the 114th Congress, she chaired the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

BG:B001300.tier_writeup: Nanette Barragán is a Democratic congresswoman from California who has voted both for and against U.S. military aid to Israel.  She cosponsored a bill limiting transfers to Israel (HR 3565) and an amendment to prohibit funding for Israel (H R 8595), but she also voted in favor of the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act (H R 8034) and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act (H R 8369).  Her record shows only one anti‑focus vote in the 119th Congress, and she has not signed any discharge petitions against her own party’s leadership.  With no significant contributions from the Israel lobby and a mixed voting history, she lacks the principled consistency required for a reliable anti‑establishment ally.  Consequently, she should be treated as a soft signal rather than a hard ally.
BG:B001300.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record is inconsistent and she has not consistently broken with her party on anti‑intervention.

A member of the Republican Party, he previously served in the United States House of Representatives from 2001 to 2019, representing two districts primarily covering North County in the San Diego area: first the 48th district for one term and then the 49th district for eight terms. From January 2011 to January 2015, he chaired the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

BG:L000593.description: Michael Ted Levin is an American politician and attorney serving as the U.S. representative for California's 49th congressional district since 2019. A member of the Democratic Party, Levin represents most of San Diego's North County, including Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, as well as a portion of southern Orange County. He is currently serving his fourth term. Levin flipped the historically Republican-held seat in 2018 after the retirement of Darrell Issa and has won four consecutive elections in the competitive district. BG:D000216.description: Rosa Luisa DeLauro is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Connecticut's 3rd congressional district since 1991. She is a member of the Democratic Party. The district is based in New Haven and includes most of its suburbs. DeLauro has been the dean of Connecticut's congressional delegation since 2013 upon the retirement of Senator Joe Lieberman.

The district, once represented by U.S. Senator Chris Murphy, comprises much of the state's northwestern portion, including New Britain, Danbury, and Waterbury. A member of the Democratic Party, Hayes became the first Black woman elected to represent Connecticut in Congress. She was recognized as the National Teacher of the Year in 2016.

BG:W000808.description: Frederica Patricia Wilson is an American politician who has been a member of the United States House of Representatives since 2011, representing Florida's 24th congressional district. Located in South Florida, Wilson's congressional district, numbered 17th during her first term, covers a large swath of eastern Miami-Dade County. The district contains most of Miami's majority-black precincts. Wilson gained national attention in 2012 for her comments on the death of Trayvon Martin. In May 2026, Wilson announced her retirement.

BG:D000600.description: Mario Rafael Díaz-Balart y Caballero is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Florida's 26th congressional district. A member of the Republican Party, he was elected in 2002, and his district includes much of northwestern Miami-Dade County, including Hialeah, and much of the northern portion of the Everglades.

BG:B000490.description: Sanford Dixon Bishop Jr. is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Georgia's 2nd congressional district since 1993. He became the dean of Georgia's congressional delegation after the death of John Lewis. A member of the Blue Dog Coalition, he belongs to the moderate faction of the Democratic Party. His district is in southwestern Georgia and includes Albany, Thomasville, and most of Columbus and Macon.

BG:L000583.description: Barry Dean Loudermilk is an American politician from the state of Georgia who has been the United States House representative from Georgia's 11th congressional district since 2015. Prior to this, Loudermilk served in the Georgia House of Representatives (2005–2010) and the Georgia Senate (2011–2013). Loudermilk stepped down from the Georgia Senate to run for Phil Gingrey's congressional seat in the 11th district.

A member of the Republican Party, Fulcher previously sought the party's nomination in the 2014 Idaho gubernatorial election, unsuccessfully challenging incumbent Butch Otter in the primary.

BG:R000617.tier_writeup: Delia Ramirez has established herself as a reliable anti-establishment voice by consistently breaking with Democratic leadership on foreign military aid and war powers. She was one of the few members to vote against the $14.3 billion Israel Security Supplemental in 2024 and has since sponsored legislation to limit the transfer of defense articles to Israel. Her record extends beyond the focus issue, as she has cosponsored multiple War Powers resolutions to remove U.S. forces from unauthorized hostilities in Lebanon, Cuba, Venezuela, and Iran. Ramirez is vocal in her opposition to the Israel lobby, publicly calling for investigations into AIPAC and denouncing the influence of billionaire donors on foreign policy. Her willingness to use the term 'genocide' regarding Gaza and her sponsorship of bills to defend Palestinian human rights demonstrate a commitment to principle over party consensus. With zero contributions from the Israel lobby and a consistent record of voting against cluster munition transfers and unauthorized deployments, she is a core ally for the coalition. She is highly likely to hold her position under pressure, given her history of aggressive rhetoric against the foreign-policy establishment.
BG:R000617.tier_bottom_line: Counts as anti-establishment because she consistently votes against military aid to Israel, sponsors legislation to block arms transfers, and challenges both parties on unauthorized military interventions.

vote_record.summary: Passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The House passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The amendment would prohibit all U.S. security assistance to Ukraine except for U.S. embassy security, effectively cutting aid to Ukraine.

The amendment would prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral exercises unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition.
On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - Amends the Foreign Military Financing Program and the National Security Investment Programs to reduce funding for Jordan by $2,100,000,000. Failed.

On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - H.Amdt. 8: Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000. Failed.
House passes a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon, passing 193-218 with 187 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 2 Republicans voting in favor.
The Ukraine Support Act authorized additional U.S. military and economic assistance for Ukraine.
The House voted to agree to H. CON. RES. 84, which would direct the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Lebanon under the War Powers Resolution; the motion failed.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove United States armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran.
The PROTECT Taiwan Act passed, directing the administration to strengthen U.S. security assistance and consider additional defensive arms sales to Taiwan.
The resolution would have directed the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela, but it failed to pass.
The resolution directed the removal of United States armed forces from hostilities in or against Venezuela that were not authorized by Congress.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere.
An amendment to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative was defeated, with 9 yeas and 213 nays.
An amendment to H.R. 3838 proposed prohibiting U.S. assistance to Ukraine, but it failed with 60 yeas and 372 nays.
The amendment repealed the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, ending those authorizations.
The amendment would have prohibited all U.S. assistance to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed with 76 yeas and 212 nays.
The amendment sought to strike funding for U.S. military assistance to Jordan.
The amendment sought to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, but it failed.
The House passed H.R. 8771, appropriating funds for the Department of State, foreign operations, and related programs for fiscal year 2025.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine, but it failed.
Amendment prohibits any foreign assistance funds in the bill from being made available to areas of Syria controlled by Bashar al-Assad, both directly and indirectly.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funds to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the United Nations unless specifically authorized by Congress, effectively restricting U.S. financial support to the UN.
The amendment bars the use of funds to administer or enforce the National Security Memorandum on safeguards and accountability for transferred defense articles and services.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the International Organization for Migration's activities in the Western Hemisphere.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Special Representative for Ukraine's Economic Recovery, cutting U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Bilateral Security Agreement between the United States and Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for foreign military sales to Ukraine, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit the transfer of cluster munitions, but it failed to pass.
The amendment prohibited any use of the Act’s funds for assistance to Ukraine.
Amendment to bar the use of funds for any NATO‑related project or activity until each member country has spent 2% of its GDP on defense; the amendment failed.
Passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which authorizes additional military aid and security assistance for Israel.
The House voted to reject a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have authorized $14 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing $14.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing approximately $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine; the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment that would have struck provisions increasing the President's authority to draw down and transfer defense articles to foreign countries.
The House passed the Standing Against Houthi Aggression Act, authorizing the use of military force against the Houthi group in Yemen to protect U.S. personnel and shipping.
The House voted down a motion to suspend the rules and pass the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would have provided additional military aid and security funding to Israel.
Passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. funds for the transfer of military equipment, training, or assistance to the Government of Iran.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from waiving statutory restrictions on arms sales to Iran, thereby blocking potential executive discretion to approve such transfers.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to provide financial assistance to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act to prohibit U.S. financial assistance to entities designated as terrorist organizations, including Hamas.

Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs for various countries including Israel and Ukraine.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce foreign assistance to countries based on the number of unaccompanied alien children entering the U.S. from those nations.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds in the bill for Pakistan.
The House voted down an amendment to the FY2024 State Department and Foreign Operations Appropriations Act that would have prohibited the use of funds to provide assistance to Iraq.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds to initiate a drawdown and delivery of defense articles and services from Department of Defense stocks to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit assistance to Ukraine, thereby allowing the aid to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce Economic Support Fund funding for Egypt and Jordan to FY2018 levels.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions.
The House voted down an amendment by Rep. Matt Gaetz that would have prohibited the provision of security assistance to Ukraine.
The vote rejected an amendment to reduce funding for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative by $300 million.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73,334,000.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program by $3 million.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the Department of Defense from providing any support to the Taliban and banning sanctions relief for Afghanistan unless explicitly authorized by Congress.

The House rejected an amendment to strike Section 217 of H.R. 2670, which would have removed authorization for funds to the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The vote failed to adopt an amendment that would have struck the provision extending lend-lease authority to Ukraine, thereby preserving the authority to provide military aid to Ukraine.
The amendment would have struck a feasibility study for creating a Center of Excellence in Ukraine, but it failed to pass.
The Gaetz amendment to H.R. 2670 sought to prohibit all security assistance for Ukraine under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
An amendment to strike $300 million in foreign military aid for Ukraine and eliminate land-lease authority for the country.
Resolution directing the President to remove all United States Armed Forces, except those protecting the U.S. Embassy, from Somalia.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from Syria under the War Powers Resolution.

The amendment would reduce the sunset provision for Section 5112(c) of the Department of State Authorization Act from two years to one year, shortening the period of U.S. security assistance authority to Ukraine.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment.

The amendment sought to cut the National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023 by $100 billion, reducing the overall authorized defense spending without changing personnel, civilian pay, benefits, or the Defense Health Program.
Provided $5.5 billion in additional military aid to Ukraine.
The Stop Iranian Drones Act, passed by the House, bans U.S. assistance and export of drone technology to Iran to curb its drone program.
The Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act authorized the use of seized Russian assets to fund reconstruction assistance for Ukraine.
Passed the Suspending Energy Imports from Russia Act, which imposed a ban on the importation of Russian oil, natural gas, and coal into the United States as a non-military economic sanction.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units involved in airstrikes causing civilian casualties in Yemen.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 4350 that terminates U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of the bill's enactment.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs globally.
The House voted to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, removing the legal authority for U.S. military operations in that country.
The House voted on a motion to recommit H.R. 256, which sought to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, effectively blocking the repeal of the war authorization.

BG:T000482.description: Lori Ann Trahan is an American businesswoman and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Massachusetts's 3rd congressional district since 2019. The district covers Boston's northwestern suburbs, and includes Lowell, Lawrence, Concord, and Trahan's hometown, Westford. A Democrat, she formerly served as chief of staff to Representative Marty Meehan in Massachusetts's 5th congressional district.

BG:C001101.description: Katherine Marlea Clark is an American lawyer and politician who has served as House minority whip since 2023 and is currently in her seventh term as the U.S. representative for Massachusetts's 5th congressional district, having held the post since 2013. vote_record.summary: Passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The House passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The amendment would prohibit all U.S. security assistance to Ukraine except for U.S. embassy security, effectively cutting aid to Ukraine.

The amendment would prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral exercises unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition.
On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - Amends the Foreign Military Financing Program and the National Security Investment Programs to reduce funding for Jordan by $2,100,000,000. Failed.

On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - H.Amdt. 8: Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000. Failed.
House passes a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon, passing 193-218 with 187 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 2 Republicans voting in favor.
The Ukraine Support Act authorized additional U.S. military and economic assistance for Ukraine.
The House voted to agree to H. CON. RES. 84, which would direct the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Lebanon under the War Powers Resolution; the motion failed.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove United States armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran.
The PROTECT Taiwan Act passed, directing the administration to strengthen U.S. security assistance and consider additional defensive arms sales to Taiwan.
The resolution would have directed the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela, but it failed to pass.
The resolution directed the removal of United States armed forces from hostilities in or against Venezuela that were not authorized by Congress.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere.
An amendment to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative was defeated, with 9 yeas and 213 nays.
An amendment to H.R. 3838 proposed prohibiting U.S. assistance to Ukraine, but it failed with 60 yeas and 372 nays.
The amendment repealed the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, ending those authorizations.
The amendment would have prohibited all U.S. assistance to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed with 76 yeas and 212 nays.
The amendment would have stripped funding for U.S. assistance to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to strike funding for U.S. military assistance to Jordan.
An amendment to cut funding for the Israeli Cooperative Programs was proposed but failed, preserving the existing aid.
The amendment sought to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, but it failed.
The House passed H.R. 8771, appropriating funds for the Department of State, foreign operations, and related programs for fiscal year 2025.
Amendment to prohibit the use of funds in the bill for acquiring, using, transferring, or selling cluster munitions.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine, but it failed.
Amendment prohibits any foreign assistance funds in the bill from being made available to areas of Syria controlled by Bashar al-Assad, both directly and indirectly.
The amendment prohibited the use of funds from the Act to support the Gaza pier, effectively blocking U.S. assistance to Hamas’s military infrastructure.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funds to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the United Nations unless specifically authorized by Congress, effectively restricting U.S. financial support to the UN.
The amendment bars the use of funds to administer or enforce the National Security Memorandum on safeguards and accountability for transferred defense articles and services.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the International Organization for Migration's activities in the Western Hemisphere.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Special Representative for Ukraine's Economic Recovery, cutting U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Bilateral Security Agreement between the United States and Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for foreign military sales to Ukraine, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit the transfer of cluster munitions, but it failed to pass.
The amendment prohibited any use of the Act’s funds for assistance to Ukraine.
Amendment to bar the use of funds for any NATO‑related project or activity until each member country has spent 2% of its GDP on defense; the amendment failed.
The House voted down an amendment to strike funding for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Security Investment Program.
Passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which authorizes additional military aid and security assistance for Israel.
The House voted to reject a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have authorized $14 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing $14.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing approximately $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine; the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment that would have struck provisions increasing the President's authority to draw down and transfer defense articles to foreign countries.
The House passed the Standing Against Houthi Aggression Act, authorizing the use of military force against the Houthi group in Yemen to protect U.S. personnel and shipping.
Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. government funds to finance the purchase of Iranian goods or services.
The House voted down a motion to suspend the rules and pass the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would have provided additional military aid and security funding to Israel.
Passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. funds for the transfer of military equipment, training, or assistance to the Government of Iran.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from waiving statutory restrictions on arms sales to Iran, thereby blocking potential executive discretion to approve such transfers.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to provide financial assistance to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act to prohibit U.S. financial assistance to entities designated as terrorist organizations, including Hamas.

Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs for various countries including Israel and Ukraine.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce foreign assistance to countries based on the number of unaccompanied alien children entering the U.S. from those nations.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds in the bill for Pakistan.
The House voted down an amendment to the FY2024 State Department and Foreign Operations Appropriations Act that would have prohibited the use of funds to provide assistance to Iraq.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds to initiate a drawdown and delivery of defense articles and services from Department of Defense stocks to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit assistance to Ukraine, thereby allowing the aid to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce Economic Support Fund funding for Egypt and Jordan to FY2018 levels.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions.
The House voted down an amendment by Rep. Matt Gaetz that would have prohibited the provision of security assistance to Ukraine.
The vote rejected an amendment to reduce funding for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative by $300 million.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73,334,000.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program by $3 million.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the Department of Defense from providing any support to the Taliban and banning sanctions relief for Afghanistan unless explicitly authorized by Congress.

The House rejected an amendment to strike Section 217 of H.R. 2670, which would have removed authorization for funds to the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The vote failed to adopt an amendment that would have struck the provision extending lend-lease authority to Ukraine, thereby preserving the authority to provide military aid to Ukraine.
The amendment would have struck a feasibility study for creating a Center of Excellence in Ukraine, but it failed to pass.
The Gaetz amendment to H.R. 2670 sought to prohibit all security assistance for Ukraine under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
An amendment to strike $300 million in foreign military aid for Ukraine and eliminate land-lease authority for the country.
Resolution directing the President to remove all United States Armed Forces, except those protecting the U.S. Embassy, from Somalia.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from Syria under the War Powers Resolution.

The amendment would reduce the sunset provision for Section 5112(c) of the Department of State Authorization Act from two years to one year, shortening the period of U.S. security assistance authority to Ukraine.

Amendment prohibits the President from selling or exporting new F‑16s or upgrade kits to Turkey unless a certification to Congress confirms the transfer is in U.S. national interest and includes safeguards against unauthorized overflights of Greece.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment.

The amendment sought to cut the National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023 by $100 billion, reducing the overall authorized defense spending without changing personnel, civilian pay, benefits, or the Defense Health Program.
Provided $5.5 billion in additional military aid to Ukraine.
The House passed a resolution to agree to consider the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would provide additional U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The Stop Iranian Drones Act, passed by the House, bans U.S. assistance and export of drone technology to Iran to curb its drone program.
The Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act authorized the use of seized Russian assets to fund reconstruction assistance for Ukraine.
Passed the Suspending Energy Imports from Russia Act, which imposed a ban on the importation of Russian oil, natural gas, and coal into the United States as a non-military economic sanction.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units involved in airstrikes causing civilian casualties in Yemen.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 4350 that terminates U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of the bill's enactment.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs globally.
The House voted to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, removing the legal authority for U.S. military operations in that country.
The House voted on a motion to recommit H.R. 256, which sought to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, effectively blocking the repeal of the war authorization.

BG:R000606.description: Jamin Ben "Jamie" Raskin is an American attorney, law professor, and politician serving as the U.S. representative for Maryland's 8th congressional district since 2017. A progressive member of the Democratic Party, he served in the Maryland State Senate from 2007 to 2016. The district previously included portions of Montgomery County, a suburban county northwest of Washington, D.C., and extended through rural Frederick County to the Pennsylvania border. Since redistricting in 2022, Raskin's district encompasses much of Montgomery County and a sliver of Prince George's County.

BG:S001215.description: Haley Maria Stevens is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative from Michigan's 11th congressional district since 2019. Elected as a member of the Democratic Party, Stevens represents most of urbanized Oakland County, including many of Detroit's northern suburbs. She ran for Michigan's Democratic nomination in the 2026 U.S. Senate election, losing to Abdul El-Sayed.

BG:T000488.description: Shrinivas Prasad Thanedar is an American businessman, author, and politician serving as the U.S. representative from Michigan's 13th congressional district since 2023. A member of the Democratic Party, Thanedar served as a member of the Michigan House of Representatives from 2021 to 2023. He was also a candidate in the Democratic primary for Governor of Michigan in the 2018 election. First elected to Congress in 2022, then again in 2024, Thanedar lost renomination in 2026 in the Democratic primary to democratic socialist Donavan McKinney.

The House passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The amendment would prohibit all U.S. security assistance to Ukraine except for U.S. embassy security, effectively cutting aid to Ukraine.

The amendment would prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral exercises unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition.
On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - Amends the Foreign Military Financing Program and the National Security Investment Programs to reduce funding for Jordan by $2,100,000,000. Failed.

House passes a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon, passing 193-218 with 187 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 2 Republicans voting in favor.
The Ukraine Support Act authorized additional U.S. military and economic assistance for Ukraine.
The House voted to agree to H. CON. RES. 84, which would direct the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Lebanon under the War Powers Resolution; the motion failed.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove United States armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran.
The PROTECT Taiwan Act passed, directing the administration to strengthen U.S. security assistance and consider additional defensive arms sales to Taiwan.
The resolution would have directed the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela, but it failed to pass.
The resolution directed the removal of United States armed forces from hostilities in or against Venezuela that were not authorized by Congress.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere.
An amendment to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative was defeated, with 9 yeas and 213 nays.
An amendment to H.R. 3838 proposed prohibiting U.S. assistance to Ukraine, but it failed with 60 yeas and 372 nays.
The amendment repealed the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, ending those authorizations.
The amendment would have prohibited all U.S. assistance to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed with 76 yeas and 212 nays.
The amendment would have stripped funding for U.S. assistance to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to strike funding for U.S. military assistance to Jordan.
An amendment to cut funding for the Israeli Cooperative Programs was proposed but failed, preserving the existing aid.
The amendment sought to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit the transfer of cluster munitions, but it failed to pass.
The amendment prohibited any use of the Act’s funds for assistance to Ukraine.
Amendment to bar the use of funds for any NATO‑related project or activity until each member country has spent 2% of its GDP on defense; the amendment failed.
The House voted down an amendment to strike funding for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Security Investment Program.
Passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which authorizes additional military aid and security assistance for Israel.
The House voted to reject a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have authorized $14 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing $14.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing approximately $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine; the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment that would have struck provisions increasing the President's authority to draw down and transfer defense articles to foreign countries.
The House passed the Standing Against Houthi Aggression Act, authorizing the use of military force against the Houthi group in Yemen to protect U.S. personnel and shipping.
Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. government funds to finance the purchase of Iranian goods or services.
The House voted down a motion to suspend the rules and pass the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would have provided additional military aid and security funding to Israel.
Passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. funds for the transfer of military equipment, training, or assistance to the Government of Iran.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from waiving statutory restrictions on arms sales to Iran, thereby blocking potential executive discretion to approve such transfers.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to provide financial assistance to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act to prohibit U.S. financial assistance to entities designated as terrorist organizations, including Hamas.

Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs for various countries including Israel and Ukraine.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce foreign assistance to countries based on the number of unaccompanied alien children entering the U.S. from those nations.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds in the bill for Pakistan.
The House voted down an amendment to the FY2024 State Department and Foreign Operations Appropriations Act that would have prohibited the use of funds to provide assistance to Iraq.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds to initiate a drawdown and delivery of defense articles and services from Department of Defense stocks to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit assistance to Ukraine, thereby allowing the aid to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce Economic Support Fund funding for Egypt and Jordan to FY2018 levels.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions.
The House voted down an amendment by Rep. Matt Gaetz that would have prohibited the provision of security assistance to Ukraine.
The vote rejected an amendment to reduce funding for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative by $300 million.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73,334,000.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program by $3 million.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the Department of Defense from providing any support to the Taliban and banning sanctions relief for Afghanistan unless explicitly authorized by Congress.

The House rejected an amendment to strike Section 217 of H.R. 2670, which would have removed authorization for funds to the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The vote failed to adopt an amendment that would have struck the provision extending lend-lease authority to Ukraine, thereby preserving the authority to provide military aid to Ukraine.
The amendment would have struck a feasibility study for creating a Center of Excellence in Ukraine, but it failed to pass.
The Gaetz amendment to H.R. 2670 sought to prohibit all security assistance for Ukraine under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
An amendment to strike $300 million in foreign military aid for Ukraine and eliminate land-lease authority for the country.
Resolution directing the President to remove all United States Armed Forces, except those protecting the U.S. Embassy, from Somalia.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from Syria under the War Powers Resolution.

The amendment would reduce the sunset provision for Section 5112(c) of the Department of State Authorization Act from two years to one year, shortening the period of U.S. security assistance authority to Ukraine.

Amendment prohibits the President from selling or exporting new F‑16s or upgrade kits to Turkey unless a certification to Congress confirms the transfer is in U.S. national interest and includes safeguards against unauthorized overflights of Greece.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment.

The amendment sought to cut the National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023 by $100 billion, reducing the overall authorized defense spending without changing personnel, civilian pay, benefits, or the Defense Health Program.
Provided $5.5 billion in additional military aid to Ukraine.
The House passed a resolution to agree to consider the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would provide additional U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The Stop Iranian Drones Act, passed by the House, bans U.S. assistance and export of drone technology to Iran to curb its drone program.
The Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act authorized the use of seized Russian assets to fund reconstruction assistance for Ukraine.
Passed the Suspending Energy Imports from Russia Act, which imposed a ban on the importation of Russian oil, natural gas, and coal into the United States as a non-military economic sanction.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units involved in airstrikes causing civilian casualties in Yemen.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 4350 that terminates U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of the bill's enactment.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs globally.
The House voted to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, removing the legal authority for U.S. military operations in that country.
The House voted on a motion to recommit H.R. 256, which sought to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, effectively blocking the repeal of the war authorization.

He was reelected for a second term in the U.S House of Representatives in 2024.

BG:T000193.description: Bennie Gordon Thompson is an American politician and educator serving as the U.S. representative for Mississippi's 2nd congressional district since 1993. A member of the Democratic Party, Thompson served as the chair of the Committee on Homeland Security from 2007 to 2011 and from 2019 to 2023. He was both the first Democrat and the first African American to chair the committee. Since 2011, he has been the only Democrat in Mississippi's congressional delegation, and since 2018 he has been the dean of the delegation after Thad Cochran left Congress.

He served as the United States secretary of the interior under president Donald Trump from 2017 until his resignation in 2019 following a series of ethics inquiries.

BG:B001298.description: Donald John Bacon is an American politician and retired military officer who has served as the U.S. representative for Nebraska's 2nd congressional district since 2017. During his 29 years in the United States Air Force, he commanded wings at Ramstein Air Base, Germany, and Offutt Air Force Base south of Omaha, Nebraska, before retiring as a brigadier general in 2014. A member of the Republican Party, his district includes all of Omaha and the areas surrounding the Offutt base.

BG:N000188.description: Donald W. Norcross is an American politician and labor leader who is the U.S. representative for New Jersey's 1st congressional district in South Jersey. A member of the Democratic Party, Norcross was first elected to this congressional seat in 2014, following the resignation of Rob Andrews. His district covers much of the New Jersey side of the Philadelphia metropolitan area, including Camden, Cherry Hill, Lindenwold, and Glassboro.

He is a member of the Democratic Party. Pallone is the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

BG:M001226.description: Robert Menendez is an American former politician and lawyer who represented New Jersey in the United States Senate from 2006 until his resignation in 2024. A member of the Democratic Party, he previously represented New Jersey's 13th congressional district in the United States House of Representatives from 1993 to 2006. His political career ended after he was convicted in a political corruption case in 2024, making him the first sitting member of Congress convicted of conspiracy to act as a foreign agent.

vote_record.summary: Passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The House passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The amendment would prohibit all U.S. security assistance to Ukraine except for U.S. embassy security, effectively cutting aid to Ukraine.

The amendment would prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral exercises unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition.
On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - Amends the Foreign Military Financing Program and the National Security Investment Programs to reduce funding for Jordan by $2,100,000,000. Failed.

On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - H.Amdt. 8: Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000. Failed.
House passes a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon, passing 193-218 with 187 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 2 Republicans voting in favor.
The Ukraine Support Act authorized additional U.S. military and economic assistance for Ukraine.
The House voted to agree to H. CON. RES. 84, which would direct the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Lebanon under the War Powers Resolution; the motion failed.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove United States armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran.
The PROTECT Taiwan Act passed, directing the administration to strengthen U.S. security assistance and consider additional defensive arms sales to Taiwan.
The resolution would have directed the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela, but it failed to pass.
The resolution directed the removal of United States armed forces from hostilities in or against Venezuela that were not authorized by Congress.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere.
An amendment to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative was defeated, with 9 yeas and 213 nays.
An amendment to H.R. 3838 proposed prohibiting U.S. assistance to Ukraine, but it failed with 60 yeas and 372 nays.
The amendment repealed the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, ending those authorizations.
The House passed H.R. 8771, appropriating funds for the Department of State, foreign operations, and related programs for fiscal year 2025.
Amendment to prohibit the use of funds in the bill for acquiring, using, transferring, or selling cluster munitions.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine, but it failed.
Amendment prohibits any foreign assistance funds in the bill from being made available to areas of Syria controlled by Bashar al-Assad, both directly and indirectly.
The amendment prohibited the use of funds from the Act to support the Gaza pier, effectively blocking U.S. assistance to Hamas’s military infrastructure.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funds to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the United Nations unless specifically authorized by Congress, effectively restricting U.S. financial support to the UN.
The amendment bars the use of funds to administer or enforce the National Security Memorandum on safeguards and accountability for transferred defense articles and services.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the International Organization for Migration's activities in the Western Hemisphere.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Special Representative for Ukraine's Economic Recovery, cutting U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Bilateral Security Agreement between the United States and Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for foreign military sales to Ukraine, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit the transfer of cluster munitions, but it failed to pass.
The amendment prohibited any use of the Act’s funds for assistance to Ukraine.
Amendment to bar the use of funds for any NATO‑related project or activity until each member country has spent 2% of its GDP on defense; the amendment failed.
The House voted down an amendment to strike funding for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Security Investment Program.
Passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which authorizes additional military aid and security assistance for Israel.
The House voted to reject a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have authorized $14 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing $14.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing approximately $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine; the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment that would have struck provisions increasing the President's authority to draw down and transfer defense articles to foreign countries.
The House passed the Standing Against Houthi Aggression Act, authorizing the use of military force against the Houthi group in Yemen to protect U.S. personnel and shipping.
Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. government funds to finance the purchase of Iranian goods or services.

The amendment would reduce the sunset provision for Section 5112(c) of the Department of State Authorization Act from two years to one year, shortening the period of U.S. security assistance authority to Ukraine.

Amendment prohibits the President from selling or exporting new F‑16s or upgrade kits to Turkey unless a certification to Congress confirms the transfer is in U.S. national interest and includes safeguards against unauthorized overflights of Greece.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of enactment.

The amendment sought to cut the National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023 by $100 billion, reducing the overall authorized defense spending without changing personnel, civilian pay, benefits, or the Defense Health Program.
Provided $5.5 billion in additional military aid to Ukraine.
The House passed a resolution to agree to consider the Additional Ukraine Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would provide additional U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The Stop Iranian Drones Act, passed by the House, bans U.S. assistance and export of drone technology to Iran to curb its drone program.
The Asset Seizure for Ukraine Reconstruction Act authorized the use of seized Russian assets to fund reconstruction assistance for Ukraine.
Passed the Suspending Energy Imports from Russia Act, which imposed a ban on the importation of Russian oil, natural gas, and coal into the United States as a non-military economic sanction.
The House agreed to an amendment requiring the suspension of U.S. sustainment and maintenance support to Saudi Air Force units involved in airstrikes causing civilian casualties in Yemen.

The House agreed to an amendment to H.R. 4350 that terminates U.S. military logistical support, spare parts transfers, and coordination efforts for Saudi and UAE-led coalition forces conducting strikes in Yemen.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the U.S. military presence in Syria without Congressional approval within one year of the bill's enactment.
Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act for FY2022, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs globally.
The House voted to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, removing the legal authority for U.S. military operations in that country.
The House voted on a motion to recommit H.R. 256, which sought to repeal the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, effectively blocking the repeal of the war authorization.

BG:S001201.description: Thomas Richard Suozzi is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for New York's 3rd congressional district since 2024 and previously from 2017 to 2023. A member of the Democratic Party, he was the county executive of Nassau County on Long Island from 2002 to 2009 and served before then as the mayor of Glen Cove for eight years. His district, which is largely suburban, includes northern Nassau County and parts of northeastern Queens.

BG:M001188.description: Grace Meng is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. representative for New York's 6th congressional district since 2013. Her district is situated within the New York City borough of Queens; it includes Bayside, East Elmhurst, Elmhurst, Flushing, Forest Hills, Fresh Meadows, Glendale, Jackson Heights, Kew Gardens, Maspeth, Middle Village, Woodside and Rego Park. A member of the Democratic Party, Meng represented the 22nd district in the New York State Assembly from 2009 until 2012. She is the first Asian American to be elected to the United States Congress from New York.

BG:K000009.description: Marcia Carolyn Kaptur is an American politician serving in her 22nd term as the U.S. representative for Ohio's 9th congressional district, having first been elected in 1983. Her district stretches across northwestern Ohio along the southern shore of Lake Erie and includes parts of Toledo and surrounding communities. She is a member of the Democratic Party.

BG:C001053.description: Thomas Jeffery Cole is an American politician and former educator serving as the U.S. representative for Oklahoma's 4th congressional district since 2003. A Republican, he previously served in the Oklahoma Senate from 1988 to 1991 and as the 26th secretary of state of Oklahoma from 1995 to 1999. An enrolled member of the Chickasaw Nation, Cole is the longest-serving Native American in the history of Congress. On April 10, 2024, Cole was elected chair of the House Appropriations Committee.

vote_record.summary: Passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The House passed a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran pursuant to the War Powers Resolution.
The amendment would prohibit all U.S. security assistance to Ukraine except for U.S. embassy security, effectively cutting aid to Ukraine.

The amendment would prohibit the Department of Defense from using taxpayer funds to cover the costs of foreign military personnel participating in bilateral or multilateral exercises unless the Secretary of Defense waives the prohibition.
On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - Amends the Foreign Military Financing Program and the National Security Investment Programs to reduce funding for Jordan by $2,100,000,000. Failed.

On Agreeing to the Amendment - H.R. 8595 - H.Amdt. 8: Amendment sought to prohibit funds appropriated by the Act from being used for Israel, and accordingly reduces the Foreign Military Financing Program account by $3,300,000,000. Failed.
House passes a resolution to remove U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon, passing 193-218 with 187 Democrats, 2 Independents, and 2 Republicans voting in favor.
The Ukraine Support Act authorized additional U.S. military and economic assistance for Ukraine.
The House voted to agree to H. CON. RES. 84, which would direct the President to remove U.S. armed forces from Lebanon under the War Powers Resolution; the motion failed.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to remove United States armed forces from hostilities with Iran under the War Powers Resolution.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities in Iran.
The PROTECT Taiwan Act passed, directing the administration to strengthen U.S. security assistance and consider additional defensive arms sales to Taiwan.
The resolution would have directed the withdrawal of U.S. armed forces from Venezuela, but it failed to pass.
The resolution directed the removal of United States armed forces from hostilities in or against Venezuela that were not authorized by Congress.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from hostilities with presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere.
An amendment to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative was defeated, with 9 yeas and 213 nays.
An amendment to H.R. 3838 proposed prohibiting U.S. assistance to Ukraine, but it failed with 60 yeas and 372 nays.
The amendment repealed the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, ending those authorizations.
The amendment would have prohibited all U.S. assistance to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed with 76 yeas and 212 nays.
The amendment would have stripped funding for U.S. assistance to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to strike funding for U.S. military assistance to Jordan.
An amendment to cut funding for the Israeli Cooperative Programs was proposed but failed, preserving the existing aid.
The amendment sought to strike funding for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, but it failed.
The House passed H.R. 8771, appropriating funds for the Department of State, foreign operations, and related programs for fiscal year 2025.
Amendment to prohibit the use of funds in the bill for acquiring, using, transferring, or selling cluster munitions.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine, but it failed.
Amendment prohibits any foreign assistance funds in the bill from being made available to areas of Syria controlled by Bashar al-Assad, both directly and indirectly.
The amendment prohibited the use of funds from the Act to support the Gaza pier, effectively blocking U.S. assistance to Hamas’s military infrastructure.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funds to the Lebanese Armed Forces, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the United Nations unless specifically authorized by Congress, effectively restricting U.S. financial support to the UN.
The amendment bars the use of funds to administer or enforce the National Security Memorandum on safeguards and accountability for transferred defense articles and services.
The amendment sought to prohibit U.S. funding for the International Organization for Migration's activities in the Western Hemisphere.
Amendment to prohibit U.S. funding for Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Special Representative for Ukraine's Economic Recovery, cutting U.S. aid to Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for the Bilateral Security Agreement between the United States and Ukraine.
The amendment sought to prohibit funding for foreign military sales to Ukraine, but it failed.
The amendment sought to prohibit the transfer of cluster munitions, but it failed to pass.
The amendment prohibited any use of the Act’s funds for assistance to Ukraine.
Amendment to bar the use of funds for any NATO‑related project or activity until each member country has spent 2% of its GDP on defense; the amendment failed.
The House voted down an amendment to strike funding for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Security Investment Program.
Passed the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which authorizes additional military aid and security assistance for Israel.
The House voted to reject a motion to recommit the Israel Security Assistance Support Act, which would have authorized $14 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing $14.3 billion in military aid to Israel.
Passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, providing approximately $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine.

The House voted on a motion to recommit the Ukraine Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2024, which would have provided $61 billion in security assistance to Ukraine; the motion failed, allowing the bill to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment that would have struck provisions increasing the President's authority to draw down and transfer defense articles to foreign countries.
The House passed the Standing Against Houthi Aggression Act, authorizing the use of military force against the Houthi group in Yemen to protect U.S. personnel and shipping.
Passed the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. government funds to finance the purchase of Iranian goods or services.
The House voted down a motion to suspend the rules and pass the Israel Security Supplemental Appropriations Act, which would have provided additional military aid and security funding to Israel.
Passed the No Funds for Iranian Terrorism Act, which prohibits the use of U.S. funds for the transfer of military equipment, training, or assistance to the Government of Iran.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the President from waiving statutory restrictions on arms sales to Iran, thereby blocking potential executive discretion to approve such transfers.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to provide financial assistance to Iran.

Passed the Hamas and Other Palestinian Terrorist Groups International Financing Prevention Act to prohibit U.S. financial assistance to entities designated as terrorist organizations, including Hamas.

Passed the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2024, which funds foreign aid and military assistance programs for various countries including Israel and Ukraine.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce foreign assistance to countries based on the number of unaccompanied alien children entering the U.S. from those nations.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds in the bill for Pakistan.
The House voted down an amendment to the FY2024 State Department and Foreign Operations Appropriations Act that would have prohibited the use of funds to provide assistance to Iraq.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds for the Lebanese Armed Forces.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds to initiate a drawdown and delivery of defense articles and services from Department of Defense stocks to Ukraine.
The House voted down an amendment to prohibit assistance to Ukraine, thereby allowing the aid to proceed.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce Economic Support Fund funding for Egypt and Jordan to FY2018 levels.
The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions.
The House voted down an amendment by Rep. Matt Gaetz that would have prohibited the provision of security assistance to Ukraine.
The vote rejected an amendment to reduce funding for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative by $300 million.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73,334,000.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program by $3 million.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the Department of Defense from providing any support to the Taliban and banning sanctions relief for Afghanistan unless explicitly authorized by Congress.

The House rejected an amendment to strike Section 217 of H.R. 2670, which would have removed authorization for funds to the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
The vote failed to adopt an amendment that would have struck the provision extending lend-lease authority to Ukraine, thereby preserving the authority to provide military aid to Ukraine.
The amendment would have struck a feasibility study for creating a Center of Excellence in Ukraine, but it failed to pass.
The Gaetz amendment to H.R. 2670 sought to prohibit all security assistance for Ukraine under the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
An amendment to strike $300 million in foreign military aid for Ukraine and eliminate land-lease authority for the country.
Resolution directing the President to remove all United States Armed Forces, except those protecting the U.S. Embassy, from Somalia.
The resolution directed the President to withdraw U.S. armed forces from Syria under the War Powers Resolution.

BG:L000602.description: Summer Lynn Lee is an American politician and social activist serving as the U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 12th congressional district since 2023. She is a member of the Democratic Party. Her district includes Pittsburgh, much of southern and eastern Allegheny County, and part of western Westmoreland County. After winning the 2022 congressional primary and the general election, Lee became the first Black woman to represent Pennsylvania in Congress.

The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions to any foreign country.
The House voted down an amendment that would have prohibited the use of funds in the bill for Pakistan.

The House rejected an amendment to prohibit the use of funds from the bill to transfer cluster munitions.
The House voted down an amendment by Rep. Matt Gaetz that would have prohibited the provision of security assistance to Ukraine.

The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program account by $73,334,000.
The House rejected an amendment to reduce the NATO Security Investment Program by $3 million.
The House agreed to an amendment prohibiting the Department of Defense from providing any support to the Taliban and banning sanctions relief for Afghanistan unless explicitly authorized by Congress.

The House rejected an amendment to strike Section 217 of H.R. 2670, which would have removed authorization for funds to the NATO Defence Innovation Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) initiative.
The House rejected an amendment that would have prohibited the sale or transfer of cluster munitions to Ukraine.
